$$
{A}^{T}\,A=[\begin{aligned}73 & 24 \\ 24 & 9\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}{v}_{11} & {v}_{12} \\ {v}_{21} & {v}_{22}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225693/assets/58c7848ab449b77040bc4e324695074f6db789cf5330c4b915cabafe6c788b49.svg)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|v_{11}|+|v_{21}|?$
current_example.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=3.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value $\sigma_1=5.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of $A^T \!A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=25.$ Computing $A^T \! A - 25 I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225693/assets/dcdf301b14990b36151cc1b8fe1bcf37f5bf5cb93c6c59d5597841434f8746df.svg)

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T\!A-25I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225693/assets/daa271a126180e135718e0cfe5f09bc6b0b754f1b97c8e1700f89bfa99f650ba.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225693/assets/0c53b687a98171b1ba33672accf26bd080f626068da7f453744b62123da88bfd.svg)

Therefore,

$$
|v_{11}|+|v_{21}| = \left| \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right| + \left| \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right| = \sqrt{2}.
$$
